problem: Most VLN-CE agents are end-to-end (recurrent memory or cross-modal attention over egocentric RGB-D frames). They must implicitly learn mapping, planning and control together. As a result they need very large amounts of experience (e.g., WPN trained on 200M steps) and never build an explicit spatial representation that language can be grounded on. Map-based alternatives such as CMTP rely on a pre-explored global topological map.
motivation: Human spatial-cognition studies suggest that landmark-based instructions are anchored onto map-like representations. The authors also find that giving the agent a local ground-truth egocentric semantic map, with no pre-exploration, markedly improves VLN-CE success. This suggests that aligning language with top-down maps is a stronger and more sample-efficient grounding than aligning it with egocentric images. In turn, the instruction can help hallucinate unobserved map regions.
key_idea: Apply cross-modal attention twice (CM²): first to predict a language-informed egocentric semantic map that hallucinates unobserved regions, then to predict the whole instructed path as a set of waypoint heatmaps on that map, which a DD-PPO PointNav controller follows.
insight: Explicit egocentric semantic maps are an effective grounding medium for language. The ground-truth local map variant (CM²-GT) reaches 52.8 SR on val-seen vs 42.9 for predicted maps, and doubling the map to 384×384 lifts SR to 58.4. This shows map quality and extent are the bottleneck. Conditioning map hallucination on the instruction helps: IoU rises 21.2→28.3, F1 33.2→42.2 and PCW 71.1→76.5 over the language-agnostic CM²-w/o-MapAttn. Gains are larger for object classes (toilet +12.4%, sink +12.6%) than for floor/wall and for waypoints near the goal. Predicting the full path at every step is ambiguous about progress, so the start-position heatmap input and the auxiliary 'waypoint already traversed' loss are essential: removing both drops CM²-GT val-seen SR from 52.8 to 29.3 (w/o start heatmap 34.3; w/o aux loss 49.1).
method: Instruction encoding: pretrained BERT (only the last layer fine-tuned) gives per-word 768-d features, projected by an FC layer to d=128.

Map encoding: a truncated ResNet18 encodes a 192×192 egocentric map (5 cm cells, 9.6 m side) into N=(h'/16·w'/16) tokens of dim 128. Separate encoders are used for the projected occupancy input and for the predicted semantic map.

Cross-modal map attention and semantic map prediction: depth is ground-projected to an occupancy grid (occupied/free/void) accumulated in a global map with Bayesian updates and cropped egocentrically. Its tokens are the query and the instruction is key/value (LXMERT-style, self-attention first, then cross-attention). The attended features H^o are concatenated at the bottlenecks of two stacked UNets: g^o predicts the full occupancy map, and g^s predicts a 27-class semantic map using a separately pretrained RGB-segmentation UNet projected to the map. Trained with pixel-wise cross-entropy against GT maps built from MP3D 3D semantics.

Cross-modal path attention and waypoint prediction: predicted-semantic-map tokens query the instruction features. The attended representation H^s plus a start-position heatmap P^0 (relative to the current pose) feed a UNet. The UNet outputs k=10 waypoint Gaussian heatmaps (σ=1, 24×24) and a per-waypoint 'already traversed' probability. Loss is visibility-masked L2 on heatmaps plus BCE for traversal; map and path losses are summed (all λ=1) and trained jointly.

Controller: picks the waypoint after the one closest to the agent as the short-term goal. An off-the-shelf DD-PPO PointNav policy (depth + goal) emits discrete actions. STOP is issued when within τ=0.5 m of the last waypoint and its heatmap confidence exceeds γ=0.6. Predictions are temporally independent (no recurrence), and the entire path is re-predicted each step.

setting.backbone: BERT (pretrained, last layer fine-tuned) + ResNet18 map encoders + cross-modal attention transformers + UNet map/waypoint predictors (trained); frozen off-the-shelf DD-PPO PointNav policy as controller
setting.training_data: ~700K samples (map + waypoint) drawn from ground-truth paths of the VLN-CE (R2R-CE) train split (~500K for CM²-GT). The RGB semantic-segmentation UNet is pretrained separately on Matterport3D RGB. GT semantic maps come from MP3D 3D semantic annotations. No augmented instruction data.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D 256×256, 90° HFOV (no panorama) + ground-truth pose
setting.action_space: predicted waypoints on egocentric map, executed by DD-PPO as low-level MOVE_FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN 15° / STOP
setting.privileged: GT agent pose from the simulator (used for map registration and DD-PPO). The CM²-GT variants additionally use the ground-truth local egocentric semantic map at test time.

results: On R2R-CE (VLN-CE) with egocentric non-panoramic RGB-D and discrete actions, CM² achieves the best val-seen SR among comparable methods: 42.9 vs LAW 40.0, CMA+PM+DA+Aug 37.0 and panoramic WPN-DD 35.0. It is near-par on val-unseen (SR 34.3 vs LAW 35.0) but has lower SPL (27.6 vs 31.0) because of longer trajectories. It gets there with only ~0.7M training samples, vs 200M steps for WPN-DD. On the test leaderboard it scores SR 31 / SPL 24, leading non-panoramic, standard-action entries on OS/SR/NE. With ground-truth local maps (CM²-GT), SR rises to 52.8 val-seen / 37.0 val-unseen, and to 58.4 val-seen with 384×384 maps.
limitations: Path is predicted from a category-level semantic map, so instruction attributes (e.g., 'brown table' vs 'red table') cannot be used to disambiguate instances. Language is only encoded via BERT with no explicit instruction decomposition.

Grounding is limited to the local egocentric map (4.8 m to each side, while the goal is ~8 m away on average). Larger maps help substantially but are computationally expensive; trajectories are long, which hurts SPL.
Relies on ground-truth simulator pose for map registration and the DD-PPO controller, and on noise-free actuation; no real-robot validation.
builds_on: Learning to Map for semantic map hallucination (Georgakis et al. 2021)
